name: envelope-wrapper
intent: Wrap an application payload in an infrastructure-compliant envelope at the messaging seam and unwrap it at the destination, so systems whose payload format cannot change can cross a channel that demands header fields, a format indicator or encryption - the payload passes through byte-for-byte while the application never sees the envelope's metadata.
problem: Two sides of a channel disagree about the message shape: the infrastructure (broker, gateway, ESB, event mesh) requires metadata - routing headers, format indicator, correlation id, security assertions, a version tag - while the application payload either cannot carry those fields or would be corrupted by them; without a place for the metadata, every sender re-invents header handling and every receiver parses the payload to find information that is not part of its domain.
context: Messaging integration over a channel with a fixed contract - brokers and event meshes, SOAP/WS-* or CloudEvents-style transports, gateway-mediated HTTP - where a payload with an established format (legacy system, published schema, party-owned document) must participate without modification, and where infrastructure metadata must be added, inspected or protected on the way. It applies whenever the application cannot be changed to emit infrastructure headers itself, whether that is technical (binary format, third-party software) or organisational (contract frozen by another party).
benefits: Existing applications participate in the integration unchanged: their payload format stays byte-for-byte what it was, all infrastructure requirements are satisfied by the envelope.
Every message on the channel has a uniform, infrastructure-compliant shape, so routing, filtering, correlation, retry and monitoring can work on metadata without understanding the payload.

Metadata concerns - authentication assertions, tracing ids, correlation ids, encryption and signing, timestamps - are added and validated in exactly one place per seam instead of in every sender and receiver.
Payload and infrastructure evolve at different speeds: the payload schema and the envelope version can be revised independently, and new header fields do not touch domain objects.
Wrappers can be layered: when a message crosses several infrastructures, each hop strips and adds its own envelope without any hop needing to understand the others' metadata.
Enables policy enforcement at the boundary - schema/format validation, security checks and auditing happen on the envelope before untrusted data reaches application code.
tradeoffs: Every hop pays an extra serialization pass and extra header bytes; for large payloads or high fan-out this is real CPU and bandwidth cost, which is why transport-native metadata (binary mode) is preferable whenever the infrastructure offers it.
A second schema exists and must be owned: the envelope version has to evolve compatibly with the payload version, and an old unwrapper meeting a new wrapper is a classic skew failure.
Authority ambiguity: the same fact can live both in transport metadata and in the body envelope (correlation id, content type, user id), and nothing in the pattern says which copy wins.
New failure surface: malformed envelopes, unwrap errors and header spoofing all become first-class bugs, and header values are attacker-controlled input that must be validated before use.
Observability regresses: channel tooling and logs see envelopes rather than payloads, so debugging requires envelope-aware tooling or an unwrapping step in the diagnostics path.

Re-encoding the payload inside a new wrapper instead of copying its bytes breaks digests and signatures and duplicates work; careless wrapping also grows nesting until no one can tell which layer owns a field.

participants.responsibility: Takes the application payload plus the metadata the infrastructure requires, builds the envelope (header section + body), and publishes it; owns the wrap function and never lets application code construct raw envelopes.

The wrapper structure itself: a header section carrying infrastructure and processing metadata (format indicator/version, correlation id, reply address, security assertions) plus a body holding the payload unchanged; possibly layered, one envelope per infrastructure.
Validates the envelope and its header fields, removes the wrapper, and hands only the payload to application code; the reverse of the wrapper and the only component that knows the envelope schema.
Transports and routes messages, requiring the compliant header fields and treating non-compliant messages as invalid; it never sees the application payload format, only the envelope.
Defines and documents the header field names, encoding and version of the envelope as a published contract shared by every wrapper and unwrapper on the channel.
Adds technical metadata (timestamps, request ids, tracing context, security tokens) to the envelope as it passes, without touching the payload; runs before dispatch and after reception.

use_cases: A legacy or third-party system that cannot emit transport headers (a mainframe job, a fixed file format, a proprietary RPC) is joined to a modern broker: the channel adapter wraps its output into envelopes and unwraps inbound ones.

Kafka or AMQP deployment where the transport demands a correlation id, content type or partition key while the domain events must stay pure: the metadata is wrapped at the outbound gateway and stripped at the inbound one.
An event mesh standardizing on CloudEvents or AsyncAPI, where every event needs the standard context attributes (id, source, type, time) around an otherwise unchanged domain payload.
Multi-hop integration where a message crosses two or more infrastructures: the sender's envelope is carried as the body of the next infrastructure's envelope and peeled hop by hop.
Transport-level security where only the envelope may be encrypted or signed (WS-Security, JWE-style wrapping) so the payload stays intact for the ultimate destination.
HTTP API gateways where authentication, tracing and rate-limit metadata must ride in headers or a metadata block while the body remains the party-owned document.

CloudEvents adoption across a multi-cloud event mesh: each cloud provider's event format is translated to a canonical CloudEvents envelope at the boundary, preserving schema and identity across clouds.

HIPAA- or PCI-compliant event streams where encryption envelope metadata, data-classification labels, and retention policy identifiers are carried in the envelope header rather than embedded in domain payloads.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant-id, partition-key, and routing-policy headers route messages to per-tenant consumer groups while the domain payload remains schema-stable across tenants.

GraphQL subscription events over a message broker: subscription metadata (subscription-id, operation-name, auth-scope) rides in the envelope while the GraphQL result payload is passed through unchanged.
gRPC streaming with envelope framing: metadata frames carry authentication tokens, call-context, and deadline headers while the streaming payload data bypasses the envelope entirely.

Serverless function event normalization (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions): the FaaS runtime injects a raw event envelope (request-id, function-name, deadline, trace-id); the adapter normalizes and strips it before passing a clean payload to the handler.
Event replay and auditing: the durable envelope (message-id, occurredAt, source, schema-version) is archived alongside the payload so that replay is semantically identical to the original emission.

Claim-check integration: an expensive or large payload is stored externally and only its reference (a SHA-256 hash, a storage key) is placed in the envelope body; the unwrapper retrieves the payload from the store before delivering it.

Apache Camel as the wrap/unwrap pair at a route boundary: SoapJaxbDataFormat marshals a JAXB payload into a SOAP envelope (and back on the server side, with header elements unmarshalled into exchange headers), and the CloudEvents component (since Camel 3.15) maps between Camel message headers and CloudEvents context attributes, so the route body stays the domain document.

WSO2 Micro Integrator proxies receive a SOAP-wrapped request, unwrap it to Plain Old XML for a backend that cannot speak SOAP, and rewrap the response - with the endpoint optionally converting between SOAP 1.1 and SOAP 1.2 envelope dialects while the business document passes through untouched.

AWS EventBridge fan-out where consumers need a stable event id for deduplication and cross-account/bus forwarding: producers wrap the domain event in a custom envelope carrying its own id, source and schema version, with the EventBridge envelope staying the outer transport layer.
avoid_when: Both ends already agree on a message contract, or the framework in use already provides the envelope (JMS Message, Spring Integration Message, WCF Message, CloudEvents SDK) - use it instead of hand-rolling a parallel one.
The payload itself must change shape to be understood - that is Message Translator, Normalizer or Converter work, not metadata wrapping.
The infrastructure already carries the metadata out of band (HTTP/2 headers, gRPC metadata, AMQP properties): binary mode is cheaper than embedding a body envelope.
The metadata is missing data the sender does not have - use Content Enricher rather than smuggling lookups into a wrapper.
The payload is large and the extra copy is prohibitive, or the message body has a hard size limit - pass a reference (Claim Check) instead of wrapping the payload.
Nothing on the channel actually consumes the metadata: wrapping without a consumer for the header fields is pure overhead.
anti_patterns: Wrapping at every layer instead of at the boundary: envelopes nested several deep, with no single owner for the header schema and a copy of the payload at each hop.

Leaking the envelope into application code: domain services parsing correlation ids or security assertions out of a wrapper type, re-coupling the application to the infrastructure the pattern was meant to hide.
Header-field soup with no schema owner: each team adds metadata ad hoc, fields collide or drift, and no one can say which header is authoritative.
Trusting envelope headers: using producer-supplied user ids, correlation ids or format indicators for authorization or dispatch without authenticating them.
Smuggling domain data into the envelope because adding a payload field requires a schema change - business facts hidden in transport metadata are invisible to the domain's own tooling.
Re-serializing the payload on every hop (wrap by decode + encode) so signatures and digests break and the envelope adds cost without adding safety.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: transport/infrastructure metadata versus domain payload, enforced by the wrapper boundary.
Information hiding: application code sees only the payload; only adapters know the envelope schema.
Single responsibility: one component wraps, one unwraps, each at its own seam.
Open/closed principle: new metadata arrives as new header fields without changing the payload schema or the domain objects.
Stable interfaces: the envelope is a published, versioned contract (a published language) shared by all producers and consumers on the channel.
Fail at the boundary: validate and reject malformed envelopes at the seam instead of propagating ambiguity into the domain.
best_practices: Wrap and unwrap exactly once per infrastructure seam, as close to the transport as possible; never let domain code construct or inspect envelopes.

Prefer the transport's own metadata channel (AMQP properties, HTTP/2 or gRPC headers, Kafka record headers, broker message properties) and fall back to a body envelope only when the infrastructure requires it.

Publish and version the envelope schema: field names, encoding, a format-indicator header (e.g. content-type, schema-id, ce-type), and a format version that lets the receiver pick the right unwrapper.
Treat every inbound header field as untrusted input: validate, bound and authenticate before use, and never derive authorization from a producer-supplied header alone.
Keep the payload opaque — copy the bytes rather than re-encoding them — so digests, signatures and encryption survive the wrap/unwrap round trip.
Decorate rather than mutate: add technical metadata (timestamps, request ids, tracing context, W3C traceparent/tracestate) through decorators at dispatch and reception, leaving the payload untouched.
Propagate W3C Trace Context headers (traceparent, tracestate) end-to-end through the envelope; generate a new traceparent only when one is absent, preserving sampling decisions from the origin.

Integrate the envelope schema with a schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue, Apicurio): register the envelope format, enforce compatibility rules, and reject incompatible schema versions at the seam.

Handle version skew explicitly: an old unwrapper encountering a new wrapper should either forward the unknown fields transparently or fail fast with a recognizable error; never silently drop new fields.
Implement idempotent unwrapping: duplicate messages with the same message-id or idempotency-key should be detected and suppressed rather than re-processed, even when the payload is identical.

Route malformed or unprocessable envelopes to a dead-letter seam or quarantine topic rather than propagating them to the application; include the full envelope (headers + body) in the dead-letter record for forensics.
Use UTF-8 or explicit binary encoding for header values; avoid ambiguous encodings that cause string-corruption when headers cross language runtimes.

Set a content-type header on the envelope that accurately reflects the body's serialization (application/json, application/xml, application/octet-stream, application/avro) so the unwrapper can deserialize without guessing.

Govern envelope header proliferation: assign an owner for the envelope schema, review new header fields for necessity and naming collisions before adding them, and deprecate unused fields on a schedule.
Test the round trip, version-skew cases (old unwrapper / new wrapper), malformed-envelope rejection, header injection attacks, and duplicate-delivery scenarios explicitly.
Log envelope metadata (message-id, correlation-id, traceparent, source) at both wrap and unwrap boundaries to enable end-to-end diagnostics without inspecting the payload.

pitfalls: Wrapping in more than one place creates nested envelopes that every hop must peel; own the wrap/unwrap pair in the adapter, never in domain code.
A header field nobody validates is a spoofing surface (correlation ids, user ids, format indicators), especially when the infrastructure does not authenticate it.
Re-encoding the payload at every hop breaks signatures and digests and doubles the serialization cost.
Envelope schema proliferation without a designated owner: each team adds header fields ad hoc, names collide or drift, and no one can say which header is authoritative for a given piece of metadata.

Time-of-check vs. time-of-use on header fields: a header that is validated at unwrap may be mutated by a subsequent middleware hop before the payload is consumed; always re-validate immediately before use.

Content-type confusion: the envelope's content-type and the payload's content-type are different fields; using the envelope's type to deserialize the payload (or vice versa) silently produces garbage data.
Over-stripping: removing intermediate-hop metadata needed for traceability (e.g., stripping traceparent when forwarding to an async consumer) breaks the distributed trace end-to-end.

Under-stripping: leaking infrastructure metadata (partition keys, internal routing tokens, broker-specific headers) to the application, coupling the domain to the transport and making future infrastructure migrations painful.
Double encoding: base64-encoding a binary payload before wrapping it in an envelope that also base64s the body, so the ultimate receiver gets a double-encoded payload that fails to deserialize.

Large envelope headers: adding bulk metadata (verbose JWTs, full SAML assertions, large JSON blobs) into header fields degrades broker throughput and can exceed broker-defined message-size limits, causing produce errors.

Envelope versioning in polyglot systems: a new header field added in one language runtime is not understood by consumers in other runtimes; without a forward-compatibility plan, unknown fields are silently dropped or cause parse errors.

Assuming correlation-id uniqueness: a correlation-id collision between two independent producers causes messages from different conversations to be incorrectly associated; combine with a globally unique message-id to detect collisions.

Signing the envelope but not the payload, or vice versa: when both transport-level and application-level signatures are in play, an attacker who controls one layer can substitute a legitimately-signed envelope containing a tampered payload.

Payload type polymorphism without a type registry: using an enum payload_type_id that collides across teams is indistinguishable from a correct type at runtime, causing silent deserialization of the wrong schema.
Ignoring envelope schema compatibility: adding a required header field to the envelope schema is a breaking change for all existing consumers; use optional fields or additive versioning instead.

Wrong move: designing one heavyweight universal envelope owned by a central platform team -> onboarding stalls, every team pays for headers it never consumes, and the envelope becomes a junk drawer where tenant-scoped metadata can leak between consumers -> instead standardize a lean envelope covering only transport, observability and security concerns and let payload extensions be owned by the domain teams.

Wrong move: using the wrapper to translate or reshape message content because it is the code you already own -> the envelope silently becomes an undocumented Message Translator and payload bugs hide inside header logic -> instead keep the wrapper a pure metadata carrier and put content transformation in a separate, named translator step.

Wrong move: hand-rolling an envelope in a homogeneous or latency-critical path where both ends already agree on the format or the framework already ships one -> you pay an extra serialization pass and a second schema for metadata no hop consumes, duplicating machinery the transport already provides -> instead integrate directly or use the transport's native headers, reserving the envelope for the seams that genuinely demand it.
